title: The Alphabet, Part Two
subtitle: N through Z, plus Ü and ß — the final sixteen.
objectives: Recognize N through Z, plus Ü and ß.
Pronounce V as [f], W as [v], Z as [ts].
Distinguish Ü from U and from the diphthong eu.
Recognize the ß (Eszett) and know when it appears.

sections.heading: The second half
sections.body: This lesson completes the alphabet. Fourteen letters remain, plus two special characters: the umlaut Ü and the ß. Three letters will surprise English speakers. V sounds like [f]. W sounds like [v]. Z sounds like [ts]. These are not exceptions — they are the rule. Once learned, they stay learned.

sections.heading: Letters N through Z, plus Ü and ß

letters.name: oh
letters.note: Short [o] as in got (but without the English [ɑ] coloring), or long [oː] as in go. Offen (short), Boot (long).

letters.name: oh-umlaut
letters.note: A front rounded vowel. Say [e] but round your lips as for [o]. Göttlich, schön. No English equivalent.

letters.name: koo
letters.note: Always followed by u, pronounced [kv]. Quelle = kvell-uh. Rare.

letters.name: err
letters.note: The German R is uvular [ʁ], a guttural sound made in the back of the throat, or rolled [r] in southern dialects. After a vowel it often vocalizes to [ɐ].

letters.name: ess
letters.note: Voiced [z] before a vowel: sagen (zah-gen). Voiceless [s] at the end or before a consonant: das (dahs), ist (ist).

letters.name: Eszett, scharfes S
letters.note: A ligature of long s + z. Always voiceless [s]. Appears after long vowels and diphthongs: Straße, groß. After short vowels, write ss: Fluss. Swiss German writes ss everywhere.

letters.name: oo
letters.note: Short or long, like the oo in boot. Mutter (short), Buch (long).

letters.name: oo-umlaut
letters.note: A front rounded vowel. Say [i] but round your lips as for [u]. Über, Tür. No English equivalent. French u in lune is the same sound.

letters.name: fow
letters.note: Usually [f]: Vater (fah-ter), Vogel (foh-gel). In foreign borrowings, sometimes [v]: Violine.

letters.name: ix
letters.note: Like English x. Rare in native words.

letters.name: üpsilon
letters.note: In German words, pronounced like Ü: Physik = fü-zeek. In foreign words, sometimes [i] or [j].

letters.name: tset
letters.note: Always [ts], like the ts in cats. Zeit (tsait), zu (tsoo). Never like English z.

sections.heading: The three surprises
sections.body:
V = [f]. Vater is pronounced fah-ter. Vogel is foh-gel. This is the old Germanic pronunciation, preserved in German and lost in English.

W = [v]. Wasser is vah-ser. Wein is vine (the drink, not the plant). The letter W in German does the work that V does in English.

Z = [ts]. Zeit is tsait. Zu is tsoo. This is the same sound as the final consonant cluster in English cats or hits. German spells it with a single letter.

sections.heading: The Eszett
sections.body:
The ß (called Eszett or scharfes S, 'sharp s') is a ligature — a fusion of two letters into one glyph. It descends from the long s (ſ) + z. It appears after long vowels and diphthongs:

  Straße (street) — long a
  groß (great) — long o
  außen (outside) — diphthong au

After short vowels, German writes ss:

  Fluss (river) — short u
  müssen (must) — short ü

The Swiss abolished the ß in 1938 and write ss everywhere. Austrian and German writers still use it. You will see both in printed texts.

sections.heading: Listening drill
sections.instructions: Each of the sixteen letters (including Ö, Ü, and ß) is spoken three times. Listen, then repeat.

sections.heading: Writing drill
sections.instructions: Print each letter ten times. The ß has no separate upper-case form in traditional typography; in all caps, write SS. Modern German has introduced a capital ẞ, but it is not yet universal.

items.prompt: What sound does the letter V make in German?
What sound does the letter W make in German?
What sound does the letter Z make in German?
When does German use ß instead of ss?
items.answer: After long vowels and diphthongs. Straße (long a), but Fluss (short u).
Say [i] but round your lips. A front rounded vowel. Like French u in lune.
Say [e] but round your lips. A front rounded vowel. No English equivalent.

items.prompt: What is the German R sound?
items.answer: Uvular [ʁ], a guttural sound from the back of the throat, or a rolled [r] in southern dialects.

sections.heading: Up next
sections.body: Lesson 1.3 covers the three umlauts together — Ä, Ö, Ü — and the historical reason they exist. After that, the consonant clusters: ch, sch, ng, pf, and the rest.

lesson_completion.criteria: Mark complete when you can pronounce V, W, Z, ß, Ü, Ö without hesitation and can read ten random German words aloud with correct sounds.
